column1: Cloudskraal Vision Framework, first draft - Purpose: align long-term direction for the Nel family and Cloudskraal
The Nel family has been farming at Cloudskraal since 1850, spanning seven generations with strong agricultural heritage and community ties.
Current transition: Pieter stepping back from operations while Nelene and Nico assume greater management responsibilities over next 3-5 years.
This document serves to align family values, business strategy, and land stewardship for sustainable multi-generational success.
Cloudskraal becomes a regenerative agricultural enterprise integrating rooibos, vineyards, and eco‑tourism under stewardship, innovation, and community prosperity.
To nurture land and family through sustainable agriculture, innovation, and a meaningful shared life on the farm.
Caring for land as a precious resource
Regenerative, diversified systems focusing on soil health, water security, and biodiversity corridors
Modernized processing, direct trade channels, and disciplined profitability
Transparent, collaborative model with clear roles and succession roadmap
Quality jobs, skills development, local value creation, and cultural heritage preservation
Transition to regenerative practices with measurable soil and water outcomes
Integrate rooibos, vineyards, eco-tourism and pilot new offerings
Define decision forums, roles and succession plan with agreed policies
Partner for employment, training and inclusive local enterprise
Prudent capital allocation, risk management and stable cash flows
Rooibos processing facility operational with improved quality and capacity
Vineyard exports double via direct trade channels
Regenerative certification achieved across core enterprises
Ian to facilitate vision alignment session
Draft MOU based on agreed vision
Define roles and scope per family member
Set metrics and cadence for quarterly/annual review
Compile source inputs: history, land baseline, financial snapshot

Feed Ratio:   Same as finishing diet, but remove additives under veterinary withdrawal regulations.Maintain high energy for minimal shrink losses.

Feed Ratio:   Roughage: 10–20%Concentrates: 80–90%Typical concentrate composition: 65–70% energy (maize, barley, oats, molasses)12–18% protein (cottonseed, soybean, lucerne meal)1–2% minerals and additives (salt, Ca:P balance, ionophores like monensin)Goals:   Rapid growth and fat deposition.Carcass dressing %: 55–65%.Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR): 5.5:1 (cattle) or 4.5:1 (sheep).

Feed Ratio:   Roughage: 30–40%Concentrates: 60–70%Target: Steady growth ( 250–350 g for sheep).Improve feed efficiency (FCR ~6:1 for cattle; 5:1 for sheep).Monitor body condition — avoid early fat deposition.

Feed Ratio:   Roughage (hay or silage): 40–60%Concentrates (grain, protein, minerals): 40–60%Notes: Start with higher roughage, gradually increase grain by 5–10% per day.Use buffers (e.g. sodium bicarbonate) to maintain rumen pH.Ensure access to clean water and good-quality roughage.

Shade Management Provide ≥ 1 m² shade per sheep (2 m² if possible).Use 80% UV-block shade cloth, not solid roofs—allow hot air to escape.Orient north–south so shade moves through the day and prevents mud.Space shade 2–3 m above ground to keep airflow.Research shows shade can drop radiant temperature by 7–10 °C (credibility 9/10).  Ventilation & Airflow Keep pens open to prevailing wind, with 3–4 m/s breeze if possible.Don’t stack solid walls; use rail fencing or mesh for cross-ventilation.For housed systems: add ridge vents, side openings, or fans (target ≥ 15 air changes/hr).Water & Feeding Adjustments Double-check trough flow—sheep can drink 10–15 L/day at 36 °C.Keep water cool and shaded; clean daily to prevent algae.Feed early morning and late evening when temps are lower.Use high-energy, lower-fermentation rations (less heat from digestion):Substitute part of the roughage with digestible fibre like lucerne pellets.Add buffers and yeast culture to stabilise rumen pH.Floor & Layout Pen slope 2–3% for drainage; avoid compacted mud that retains heat.If possible, wet surfaces lightly (spray) during hottest hours—but avoid soaking animals (risk of humidity spike).Monitoring Watch respiration rate:Normal = 20–30 breaths/min.Heat stress = > 60 breaths/min → take action.Provide emergency cooling: misting or shade tunnels.
